bio.en: Elizabeth Stone is the chief technology officer at Netflix—reportedly the first economist ever named CTO of a Fortune 500 company—and previously held leadership roles in data and science at Netflix, Lyft, and Nuna.
bio.zh: Elizabeth Stone 是 Netflix 的首席技术官——据称是有史以来第一位出任财富 500 强公司 CTO 的经济学家，此前曾在 Netflix、Lyft 和 Nuna 担任数据与研究领域的领导职务。

summary.en: Elizabeth explains how her economics background shaped her career and why she expects more economists to rise in tech leadership, and shares her 'secret sauce' for consistently climbing quickly across companies. She walks through Netflix's distinctive culture of high talent density, radical candor, and freedom and responsibility, and how that culture is the foundation everything else rests on. The conversation also covers how Netflix structures its data and user-research teams, and what endurance sports like triathlons have taught her about work and life.
summary.zh: Elizabeth 解释了经济学背景如何塑造了她的职业生涯，以及为何她预计会有更多经济学家进入科技公司的领导层，并分享了她能在多家公司快速晋升的“秘诀”。她梳理了 Netflix 以高人才密度、极致坦诚、自由与责任为核心的特殊文化，以及为何这种文化是其他一切的根基。对话还涵盖了 Netflix 如何组织其数据与用户研究团队，以及铁人三项等耐力运动教会她的关于工作与人生的道理。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: We can't really have any of the other aspects of the culture, including candor, learning, seeking excellence in improvement, freedom and responsibility if you don't start with high talent density. And in some ways, it's very reflective of Reed Hastings as founder of Netflix. So when he founded Netflix and grew the company over time, it was with a belief that there could be a different approach to building a company that would make it a place that people thrived in and loved being and would feel different than other places, both in the quality of that talent density, but even more importantly, the excellence and the outcomes. And that that's where people would derive a lot of sense of fulfillment. So it is very deeply seated at Netflix from its original days. And in order to do that, you have to really hold yourself to a lot of stuff that doesn't feel like natural human behavior.
turns.zh: 如果你不从高人才密度开始，我们就无法真正拥有这种文化的任何其他方面，包括坦诚、学习、追求卓越的改进、自由和责任。在某些方面，这非常反映了作为 Netflix 创始人的里德·黑斯廷斯 (Reed Hastings)。因此，当他创立 Netflix 并随着时间的推移不断发展公司时，他相信可以采用不同的方法来建立一家公司，使其成为一个让人们茁壮成长、热爱存在的地方，并在人才密度的质量上，更重要的是在卓越和成果上，给人一种与其他地方不同的感觉。这就是人们可以获得很多成就感的地方。因此，从最初的时候起，它就在 Netflix 中根深蒂固。为了做到这一点，你必须真正让自己坚持很多不符合人类自然行为的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So when we booked this conversation, you are VP of data in Netflix. And since then you got a promotion, you're now the CTO of Netflix, which feels significantly more fancy. Question for you, what is life like now that you are CTO versus VP of data? How is it most different? I'm imagining more meetings.
turns.zh: 因此，当我们预订这次谈话时，您是 Netflix 的数据副总裁。从那时起，你得到了晋升，现在你是 Netflix 的首席技术官，这感觉明显更高级。问你一个问题，现在你担任首席技术官和数据副总裁，生活是什么样的？它有何不同？我正在想象更多的会议。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: I would say the biggest thing that changed is probably the amount of context switching and the degree to which I feel behind or I have a lot to learn. And I felt like I had a lot to learn in the VP of data and insights role that I was in before in part because we cover a lot of different areas of the business and there's always people to learn from, but the engineering organization just takes that to 100 basically. So more people to get to know, more problem spaces, aspects of technical expertise that I'm just not as deeply familiar with. And yeah, a lot more meetings.
turns.zh: 我想说最大的变化可能是上下文切换的数量以及我感觉落后的程度或者我有很多东西需要学习。我觉得在我之前担任的数据和洞察副总裁职位上，我有很多东西需要学习，部分原因是我们涵盖了许多不同的业务领域，并且总有值得学习的人，但工程组织基本上只是将其扩展到 100 人。因此需要认识更多的人、更多的问题空间、更多我不太熟悉的技术专业知识。是的，还有更多的会议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine many higher stakes meetings as well.
turns.zh: 我想象还有许多更高风险的会议。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yes. So thankfully not a lot of meetings that Netflix feel like now you're really in this scary room, but it does feel like the role has more consequence, which is actually an exciting thing.
turns.zh: 是的。值得庆幸的是，Netflix 并没有太多的会议让你感觉现在真的在这个可怕的房间里，但确实感觉这个角色有更多的后果，这实际上是一件令人兴奋的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind along the lines of what you just talked about being a CTO. Your background is actually unusual. You're a trained economist, you got a PhD in economics. And from what I can tell, you're the first CTO of Fortune 500 company that is an economist trained in economics. First of all, is that true? I don't know if I think that's true, but you tell me.
turns.zh: 就像您刚才谈到的 CTO 一样。你的背景其实很不寻常。你是一位训练有素的经济学家，你获得了经济学博士学位。据我所知，您是财富 500 强公司中第一位受过经济学训练的经济学家 CTO。首先，这是真的吗？我不知道我是否认为这是真的，但你告诉我。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: I have not checked the list. That was one of the things I did not do after getting the title. It might be unusual. I've heard a lot of feedback on that, so I don't know if I'm the one and only, but I will definitely say it's probably unusual.
turns.zh: 我还没有检查过名单。这是我获得冠军后没有做的事情之一。这可能是不寻常的。我听到了很多对此的反馈，所以我不知道我是否是唯一的，但我肯定会说这可能很不寻常。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So I guess the question is just, do you think this is an anomaly and going to continue to be really rare? Do you think this some are going to see more at tech companies? And generally do you think tech companies should hire more economists?
turns.zh: 是的。所以我想问题只是，你认为这是一种异常情况并且会继续非常罕见吗？您认为科技公司会更多地看到这种情况吗？一般来说，您认为科技公司应该雇用更多经济学家吗？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yes to the last question. That's the easiest of it. But one of the things I observed even with the focus on data science where I've been deeper for a period of time is that economics is a flavor of data science. So it is a set of technical skills for sure. It's a way of framing certain problems or solving challenges. (00:07:06): And so when I was first switching from economics into tech, it was before there was a lot of sort of the frenzy around data science that we've seen more recently and it was harder to make that argument that economics is a flavor of data science and maybe complimentary to other versions of data science. And I feel more strongly about that now that I've seen it up close. And so maybe by extension I would say just like I think data science can be helpful for a lot of different problems that you might not immediately think, "Oh, this is something that we should bring data to," I think that economics is generally valuable for a lot of different challenges and it's a useful perspective to add to things, especially in a business context and especially in how we want to simplify problems in a way that makes them feel tractable. (00:08:00): So I feel like that's been a benefit to me to have had that type of formal training and then bring that perspective or way of thinking to different roles. And so I don't know that many people at Netflix think of me as an economist, but I find it comes out in the way I think about things. So to the extent that that's true generally, I think it's useful in a lot of companies. And I feel like even since I made the switch towards tech, I've seen it become much, much more common to think about the value of having economists on teams.
turns.zh: 是的，最后一个问题。这是最简单的。但我观察到的一件事是，即使我专注于数据科学，我已经深入研究了一段时间，但经济学是数据科学的一种风格。所以它肯定是一套技术技能。这是构建某些问题或解决挑战的一种方式。 (00:07:06)：所以当我第一次从经济学转向科技时，我们最近看到了数据科学的狂热，很难提出经济学是数据科学的一种风格并且可能与其他版本的数据科学互补的论点。现在我近距离看到了它，对此我的感受更加强烈。因此，也许通过扩展，我会说，就像我认为数据科学可以帮助解决许多不同的问题一样，你可能不会立即想到，“哦，这是我们应该用数据来解决的问题，”我认为经济学对于许多不同的挑战通常是有价值的，并且它是一个有用的视角，可以添加到事物中，特别是在商业环境中，特别是在我们希望如何以一种让问题变得易于处理的方式简化问题时。 (00:08:00)：所以我觉得接受这种正式培训然后将这种观点或思维方式带到不同的角色对我来说是有好处的。因此，我不知道 Netflix 中有多少人认为我是一名经济学家，但我发现这体现在我思考事物的方式上。因此，就一般情况而言，我认为它对很多公司都很有用。我觉得，自从我转向科技行业以来，我发现思考团队中经济学家的价值变得越来越普遍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to pull on that thread a little bit more, is there something very tactical or concrete that you can share that you find helpful with that background that you found helpful in your career?
turns.zh: 只是为了进一步拉动这个线索，是否有一些非常战术性或具体的东西可以分享，您认为这些内容对您认为对您的职业生涯有帮助的背景有帮助？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Other than the dismal dry science of it all? So one example would probably be in an understanding incentives and thinking about unintended consequences. I think that that is true both in terms of internal leadership, so being part of a management team that's thinking about how do we clarify priorities or motivate a company or define the problems we want to solve. And then part of it is more externally oriented. How do we want to think about what Netflix is to consumers and how we want to think about competition? (00:09:24): There can be a rational way of thought, which is one version of economics of shouldn't rational intelligent people behave in the following way. And then there's the, well, if given certain incentives, what might you see that we didn't think was optimal or we weren't expecting to happen but could be a consequence or repercussion here? And so I think that that type of framing, I don't know if it's unique to economics in a way because it has elements of psychology to it as well and planning ahead has become really useful for thinking through cause and effect. So that has come up in a lot of different spaces in Netflix and in other roles I've been in.
turns.zh: 除了这一切令人沮丧的枯燥科学之外？因此，一个例子可能是理解激励因素并思考意想不到的后果。我认为这对于内部领导力而言都是如此，因此作为管理团队的一部分，我们正在思考如何澄清优先事项或激励公司或定义我们想要解决的问题。然后一部分是更加面向外部的。我们如何看待 Netflix 对消费者的意义以及如何看待竞争？ (00:09:24)：可能存在一种理性的思维方式，这是经济学的一个版本，理性的聪明人不应该以下列方式行事。然后，如果给予一定的激励，你可能会看到什么是我们认为不是最佳的或者我们没有预料到会发生但可能会产生后果或影响的事情？所以我认为这种类型的框架，我不知道它在某种程度上是否是经济学所独有的，因为它也有心理学的元素，提前计划对于思考因果关系变得非常有用。所以这在 Netflix 的很多不同领域以及我担任过的其他角色中都出现过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was looking at your LinkedIn and looking at your career over the years. It seems like you've had a meteoric rise at four different companies. And I'll just walk through them briefly. So at your first job, you went from associate to vice president in three years. At the next company, Nuna, you went from manager of data science to COO in two years. At Netflix you went from VP to CTO in three years. I think that's really rare. I'm curious what is your secret sauce to being so successful at so many places and especially in the context of what advice can you share with folks earlier in their career?
turns.zh: 我一直在查看你的 LinkedIn 并查看你这些年来的职业生涯。看起来你在四家不同的公司都获得了飞速的晋升。我将简要介绍一下它们。因此，在您的第一份工作中，您在三年内从助理晋升为副总裁。在下一家公司 Nuna，您在两年内从数据科学经理晋升为首席运营官。在 Netflix，您在三年内从副总裁晋升为首席技术官。我认为这确实很少见。我很好奇您在如此多的地方取得如此成功的秘诀是什么，特别是您可以与职业生涯早期的人们分享哪些建议？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: This is one of those questions that sparks the reflection that I wouldn't normally do, so that's great. I really don't think of it as a secret sauce, but maybe I can walk through some of the things that I think have been instrumental. As you listed that out, it sounds like the two to three year point is the real sweet spot, so maybe there's something about that timeline. But I think some things almost feel trite in how I would say them, which is I'm very dedicated to the work and to the teams I'm part of. It's been part who I am for a long time that I give everything I've got to the job that I'm in. And I think that dedication and that I get joy out of that has mattered. It matters because I enjoy what I'm doing. I do the best work I possibly can, less so for myself and my own ambition and more so because I think of myself as being part of a team and so I really need to deliver for that team. (00:11:52): I think that framing in my mind and that motivation has helped me in a few fronts, which is the way in which I build partnerships with people I work with that I really care about setting other people up for success and being someone that people want to work with, so I learn from them, they learn from me, and we get better outcomes for the business together, I have found that part of that is being someone that people can leverage to translate from technical to non-technical and non-technical to technical. So that I do think has been a relative advantage in my role. So while I was often sitting in more technically-oriented teams, a lot of the advancement in my career was to roles that required that type of communication fluency. It grew out of being able to partner with people across the businesses who didn't necessarily have the same background, but where we needed to really connect spaces so that we could be more effective. (00:12:57): That was something that I think really the training for that came from analysis group where it was a very quantitative set of work that we had to find a way to communicate to judges and juries for economic cases. So that was something that was trained in other roles and I think I've been able to leverage. I'm a relatively introverted only child, so I observe a lot, which means that I learned from other people. And in each of these roles I have tried really hard to watch what other people are doing, think about how could I learn something from them, whether it's the thing that I want to be able to do myself or it's the thing that I think, "Oh, that doesn't quite fit or feel authentic with my style." And I do a lot of that introspection. So I have been surrounded by amazing people in all these roles and I have a feeling that I learned a lot by osmosis and observation and then have been able to leverage that to be stronger in the roles I was sitting in.
turns.zh: 这是引发我通常不会做的反思的问题之一，所以这很好。我真的不认为这是一个秘密武器，但也许我可以逐步介绍一些我认为有用的事情。正如您所列出的那样，听起来两到三年的时间点是真正的最佳时机，所以也许这个时间表有些道理。但我认为有些事情在我的表达方式上几乎感觉陈词滥调，那就是我非常专注于工作和我所属的团队。很长一段时间以来，我为自己所从事的工作付出了我所拥有的一切，这已经成为我的一部分。我认为奉献精神以及我从中获得的快乐很重要。这很重要，因为我喜欢我正在做的事情。我尽我所能，尽我所能，不是为了我自己和我自己的野心，而是因为我认为自己是团队的一部分，所以我真的需要为该团队做出贡献。 (00:11:52)：我认为我头脑中的框架和动机在几个方面帮助了我，这就是我与同事建立伙伴关系的方式，我真的很关心让其他人取得成功，并成为人们愿意与之合作的人，所以我向他们学习，他们向我学习，我们一起为业务取得更好的成果，我发现其中一部分是成为人们可以利用的人，将技术转化为非技术和非技术到技术。所以我确实认为这是我的角色的相对优势。因此，虽然我经常坐在更注重技术的团队中，但我职业生涯中的很多进步都是针对需要这种流畅沟通的角色。它源于能够与不同企业的人员合作，这些人员不一定具有相同的背景，但我们需要真正连接空间，以便我们能够更加有效。 (00:12:57)：我认为这确实是来自分析小组的培训，这是一组非常定量的工作，我们必须找到一种方法与经济案件的法官和陪审团进行沟通。所以这是在其他角色中接受过的培训，我想我已经能够利用了。我是一个比较内向的独生子，所以我观察很多，这意味着我向别人学习。在每一个角色中，我都非常努力地观察其他人在做什么，思考我如何才能从他们身上学到一些东西，无论是我希望自己能够做的事情还是我认为“哦，这不太适合我的风格或感觉不太真实”的事情。我做了很多内省。因此，我周围都是担任所有这些职位的出色人士，我有一种感觉，通过潜移默化和观察，我学到了很多东西，然后能够利用这些知识在我所担任的职位上变得更强。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I took a few notes here. A few things you mentioned is just like, dedication, essentially working really hard and taking your work seriously, being part of a team and setting other people up for success, translating complex tech language and problems to non-tech people, and then being really good at observing and learning from other people around you. Is there an example or two that you could share of some of these to make it even more concrete for people? Like dedication. Is that just like working many hours, being part of a team? Anything along those lines to share a story maybe to help people put this into practice.
turns.zh: 我在这里做了一些笔记。你提到的一些事情就像，奉献精神，本质上是非常努力工作并认真对待你的工作，成为团队的一员并帮助其他人取得成功，将复杂的技术语言和问题翻译给非技术人员，然后非常善于观察并向周围的其他人学习。您是否可以分享其中的一两个例子，以使其对人们来说更加具体？喜欢奉献。这就像工作很多时间、成为团队的一员一样吗？任何分享故事的内容都可能有助于人们将其付诸实践。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: No, and it's a good clarification because the dedication piece really isn't about long working hours. It's more about how much I care about excellence, I guess. So giving it my best in those situations. And that might not mean that I work really wild hours or I work weekends or I'm the one who's willing to sacrifice the vacation. I've actually tried to avoid setting that as an expectation, but more that I hold myself to a very high standard. (00:15:13): So an example would be, especially as I've gotten more senior in roles, there can be an expectation that it's okay for other people to wait on me. So whether it's the timing for a meeting or providing input on something or reviewing a document or following through on something I said that I was going to do, and I really try to avoid that, which means that if someone sends me something, I try to be very responsive about it. If I know that I said I'm going to do something, I follow through on it in the timeline that I said I was going to do. If I have a meeting, I try to be on time to that meeting. (00:16:01): Those are all flavors of dedication to the work that show up in, "Oh, it seems like Elizabeth works really hard," but the motivation factor is other people are relying on me and I want to show up for them. And so that's when I say dedication and it's related to the second point around showing up well for the team, those would all be examples of I feel urgency in responding to people and doing high quality work. (00:16:27): For the other parts of technical to non-technical, I think a great example is actually a very timely one at Netflix, which is, we are making strides to offer live content types. So live events, live TV shows. We announced this week that we're going to be hosting WWE starting later this year and early next year, 2025. That is easier said than done. I know that there's a lot of entertainment companies that have live content. But Netflix has really been in the streaming content business, so live content is something new for us and it's something that's going to require a really close partnership between our content organization and our products and technology organization because there's a content strategy to it, there's a business strategy, there's a technology strategy to it. A big part of my role is, can I explain how we're going to approach those technical problems in a way that builds competence with the content team? Can I try to understand their content strategy in a way that sets the technical teams up for success and we understand what we need to be able to deliver on here in terms of requirements. (00:17:46): I don't think I'd be able to do my current role well if I wasn't able to do that type of translation for something that's going to be a big bet for the business and something we want to invest in jointly. And then to set my partners up for success in that. So I am going to do everything I can to make sure we deliver well for my content partners because I feel like that's what's best for Netflix in the business.
turns.zh: 不，这是一个很好的澄清，因为奉献精神实际上并不是关于长时间工作。我想，更多的是我对卓越的关心程度。所以在这种情况下我会尽力而为。这可能并不意味着我工作时间非常疯狂，或者我周末工作，或者我是那个愿意牺牲假期的人。事实上，我试图避免将其设定为一种期望，但更多的是我对自己要求很高的标准。 (00:15:13)：举个例子，尤其是当我的职位越来越高时，可能会期望其他人可以侍候我。因此，无论是开会的时间、提供意见、审查文件还是落实我说我要做的事情，我都会尽力避免这种情况，这意味着如果有人给我发了一些东西，我会尽力做出回应。如果我知道我说过我要做某事，我就会按照我说过的时间表去做。如果我有会议，我会尽量准时参加会议。 (00:16:01)：这些都是对工作的奉献精神，表现在“哦，看来伊丽莎白工作真的很努力”，但动力因素是其他人依赖我，我想为他们服务。所以当我说奉献精神时，它与为团队表现良好的第二点有关，这些都是我在回应人们和做高质量工作方面感到紧迫的例子。 (00:16:27)：对于技术到非技术的其他部分，我认为 Netflix 的一个很好的例子实际上是一个非常及时的例子，也就是说，我们正在大力提供直播内容类型。所以现场活动，现场电视节目。我们本周宣布，我们将在今年晚些时候和明年初（2025 年）举办 WWE。说起来容易做起来难。我知道有很多娱乐公司都有直播内容。但 Netflix 确实涉足流媒体内容业务，因此直播内容对我们来说是新事物，这需要我们的内容组织、产品和技术组织之间建立非常密切的合作伙伴关系，因为它有内容策略、业务策略和技术策略。我的一个重要职责是，我能否解释一下我们将如何以培养内容团队能力的方式解决这些技术问题？我是否可以尝试以一种让技术团队取得成功的方式理解他们的内容策略，并且我们了解我们需要能够根据需求在这里交付什么。 (00:17:46)：如果我不能为对企业来说是一个很大的赌注以及我们想要共同投资的东西进行这种类型的翻译，我认为我无法很好地胜任目前的角色。然后让我的合作伙伴在这方面取得成功。因此，我将尽我所能，确保我们为我的内容合作伙伴提供良好的服务，因为我觉得这对 Netflix 的业务来说是最好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing examples. In terms of life content, I think about the Love is Blind. I think it was for premier, whatever, reunion that we got sucked into that show. So good job. And I think there were some issues with that, right? That reunion streak.
turns.zh: 令人惊奇的例子。就生活内容而言，我想到了《爱情是盲目的》。我想我们是为了首映，不管怎么说，重聚才被卷入那个节目的。干得好。我认为这存在一些问题，对吗？那次重逢。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Well, yeah, that was about a little less than a year ago now. So the amazing thing about failure is you learn a lot. We learned a lot. We've taken notes on it and we had a couple successful events after that, including the Netflix Cup last October. And we've got some exciting events coming up. So I think that's something that strengthened us, but did reveal that we're tackling a hard problem.
turns.zh: 嗯，是的，那是大约不到一年前的事了。所以失败的惊人之处在于你可以学到很多东西。我们学到了很多。我们对此做了记录，此后我们举办了几场成功的活动，包括去年 10 月的 Netflix 杯。我们即将举办一些激动人心的活动。所以我认为这增强了我们的力量，但也表明我们正在解决一个难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, the Twitter feeds during that, Love is Blind premiere were hilarious. People are pissed. (00:18:57): Okay. And then in terms of the, keeping a high bar for yourself, I love that. I think about a quote that... There's a VC, Ann Miura-Ko, at Floodgate and she did this interview with Tim Ferris. She shared that her dad always asked her, "Are you doing a World-class job with this? Are you doing a world-class job with your homework? Are you doing a world-class job with your piano recital?" And that's the bar that he always had for her. And I feel like that's a really good way to think about work and life in general if you can.
turns.zh: 是的，《Love is Blind》首映期间的 Twitter 消息非常搞笑。人们很生气。 (00:18:57)：好的。然后就为自己保持高标准而言，我喜欢这一点。我想到了一句话……Floodgate 有一位 VC，Ann Miura-Ko，她接受了 Tim Ferris 的采访。她分享说，她的父亲总是问她：“你的作业达到了世界一流水平吗？你的家庭作业达到了世界一流水平吗？你的钢琴演奏会达到了世界一流水平吗？”这就是他一直为她设立的酒吧。我觉得如果可以的话，这是思考工作和生活的一个非常好的方式。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah, my mother used to describe to me, probably still does, though it required more repeating when I was younger, that the last 5% is the 5% that really mattered. And so it is that framing of the extra effort you put into something to make it world-class or to make it excellent. And so I do like to push myself that way and I hope it sets a good example for other people too. It's very consistent with especially the company cultures that I tend to thrive in where that's the general expectation of the culture. So you don't feel like you're doing it alone, because then I think you can start to feel frustrated by that.
turns.zh: 是的，我母亲曾经向我描述过，也许现在仍然如此，尽管在我年轻的时候需要更多地重复，最后 5% 才是真正重要的 5%。因此，它是你为某件事付出额外努力以使其成为世界一流或使其变得优秀的框架。所以我确实喜欢这样推动自己，我希望这也能为其他人树立一个好榜样。这与我倾向于蓬勃发展的公司文化非常一致，尤其是在这种文化的普遍期望中。所以你不会觉得你是一个人在做这件事，因为我认为你会开始感到沮丧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that this is a big part of Netflix culture and I want to get into it. But before that, I'm curious just what that looks like with people that report to you. How do you help them level up in this skill of having a really high bar? And an example I'll give as you think about maybe an example is the way I described this to my PMs was, you want to have this aura that you've got this that, "If you give Lenny something, he's got this. He's going to follow up, he's going to close the loop, he's going to get it done. If he can't get it done, he'll tell me, I feel like this thread will not disappear. He won't drop this ball." Is there anything that you've learned as a good way to help someone learn this kind of skill, understand why this is so important?
turns.zh: 我知道这是 Netflix 文化的重要组成部分，我想参与其中。但在此之前，我很好奇向你汇报的人是什么样的。您如何帮助他们提高这项具有很高标准的技能？我会举一个例子，你可能会想到，我向我的产品经理描述这一点的方式是，你想要拥有这样的光环，“如果你给莱尼一些东西，他就会得到这个。他会跟进，他会关闭循环，他会完成它。如果他不能完成它，他会告诉我，我觉得这条线不会消失。他不会放弃这个球。”您是否学到了什么可以作为帮助某人学习此类技能并理解为什么这如此重要的好方法？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: It shows up for the people who report to me, is one part example setting. So if I don't do it, why would they do it? I treat that very seriously that we should all be held to the same standards. (00:21:12): And as a second thing, I give feedback when it's not up to the standard. So I think one of the things I've observed especially with people on my teams is that the expectations aren't always clear and you can't assume that they're clear if you don't share them. When something's not meeting expectations or really showing up as excellence, I think it's a combination of both giving the feedback on that and being direct about it and being specific about what would it take to get this to the bar that I am expecting or to show up in the way that I'm expecting. (00:21:55): And then the third and probably most important thing is help them fill that gap. So that would mean... Let's take an example. It certainly has happened frequently in many jobs. A document is okay, it's not great, it's not going to be easy for people to follow, it's not as crisp as it could be. There's things that would strengthen it. I can both give the feedback on that to make sure like, yes, it's going to take another round of iteration, yes, we're going to have to work another week on this and not be done with it, but pushing people to get there, and then jumping into the document and helping. (00:22:32): So I feel very strongly about, and that's kind of what I mean by setting an example of like, "Let's work on this together," and then through that, help people uplevel themselves so the next time around they know the expectations and they've had help getting there in the past. So that's probably happened a thousand times in my career where I jump in with both feet because something needs to be better and I think the teams are better for it afterwards, or I hope they are.
turns.zh: 它向我报告的人显示，是示例设置的一部分。那么如果我不这样做，他们为什么要这么做呢？我非常严肃地对待这一点，我们都应该遵守相同的标准。 (00:21:12)：第二件事是，当不符合标准时我会提供反馈。所以我认为我观察到的一件事，特别是与我的团队成员一起，期望并不总是明确的，如果你不分享它们，你就不能假设它们是明确的。当某件事没有达到预期或没有真正表现出卓越时，我认为这是提供反馈和直接反馈的结合，并具体说明如何才能使其达到我期望的标准或以我期望的方式出现。 (00:21:55)：第三件事，可能也是最重要的事情是帮助他们填补这一空白。所以这意味着......让我们举个例子。这种情况在很多工作中确实经常发生。文档还可以，但不是很好，人们不容易理解，也不够清晰。有些东西可以加强它。我都可以提供反馈，以确保，是的​​，这将需要另一轮迭代，是的，我们将不得不再工作一周，而不是完成它，而是推动人们到达那里，然后跳入文档并提供帮助。 (00:22:32)：所以我对此感觉非常强烈，这就是我的意思，我要树立一个榜样，“让我们一起努力解决这个问题”，然后通过这个例子，帮助人们提升自己，这样下一次他们就会知道期望，并且他们在过去已经得到了帮助来实现这一目标。因此，在我的职业生涯中，这种情况可能发生过一千次，我双脚投入，因为有些事情需要变得更好，我认为球队之后会变得更好，或者我希望他们是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's such a good framework just to kind of mirror back what you said, "Set expectations that the bar is going to be really high and here's what I'm expecting from you." Give them very specific feedback on where the gap is and then help them fill that gap. I think a lot of people may feel this and hear this and they're like, "Oh man, I don't want a manager that's like this high of an expectation person and it just feels really stressful." But I've had these managers and I feel like that's when I've learned the most and leveled up the most, is having someone that had really high expectations and then helped me understand, "Here's where you're not doing as well as you can. I know you can do better. Go back and work on this." I know that sounds annoying, but I think in practice it ends up helping you most in your career. I imagine you've seen a similar result.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个很好的框架，正好可以反映您所说的“设定很高的期望，这就是我对您的期望”。就差距所在向他们提供非常具体的反馈，然后帮助他们填补这一差距。我想很多人可能都会感受到这一点并听到这一点，他们会说，“哦，伙计，我不想要一个对人有如此高期望的经理，而且感觉压力很大。”但我有过这些经理，我觉得那是我学到最多、提升最多的时候，就是有人对我抱有很高的期望，然后帮助我理解，“这就是你做得不够好的地方。我知道你可以做得更好。回去继续努力吧。”我知道这听起来很烦人，但我认为在实践中它最终对你的职业生涯有最大的帮助。我想您也看到过类似的结果。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: I think so. I mean you'd have to ask some of the people on my team. So I might look at it differently that they look at it.
turns.zh: 我想是的。我的意思是你必须询问我团队中的一些人。所以我可能会以不同的方式看待它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:23:52] differences.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: It's a hard skill because it's not always easy to give feedback, especially if you feel like you know someone's put a lot of effort into something. And so I give a lot of thought to how I deliver that feedback so it feels like we're on the same team and I'm trying to help them be successful, not to help encourage failure. And that's where I think that third piece of the framework of jumping in to help can make people feel like, "I'm in a safe space. My manager wants me to be successful. My manager's helping me here." I do often do that behind the scenes. So maybe that's another flavor of this, which is, I don't do it live in the big meeting in front of all the people where the presentation doesn't go very well. I do it afterwards where it feels like a safer space to say, "Here's a way this could have gone better. Let's think about this differently next time." So it gives people a little grace and a little bit of an ability to absorb that feedback without feeling like it's kind of on a stage.
turns.zh: 这是一项硬技能，因为提供反馈并不总是那么容易，尤其是当你觉得你知道某人在某件事上付出了很多努力时。因此，我对如何提供反馈进行了很多思考，这样感觉就像我们在同一个团队中，我正在努力帮助他们成功，而不是帮助鼓励失败。这就是我认为介入帮助框架的第三部分可以让人们感觉，“我在一个安全的空间。我的经理希望我成功。我的经理在这里帮助我。”我经常在幕后这样做。所以也许这就是另一种风格，那就是，我不会在大型会议上当着所有人的面进行现场演示，因为那里的演示进展得不太顺利。之后我会在感觉更安全的地方说：“这是一种可以做得更好的方法。下次让我们以不同的方式思考这个问题。”因此，它给人们带来了一点优雅和一点能力来吸收反馈，而不会感觉像是在舞台上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another thing someone may be feeling when they're hearing this is like, "Oh my god, it's going to take me so many hours to just get it to a place Elizabeth is happy with." And I know you said that this doesn't mean necessarily many hours. Do you have any advice or thoughts on just how to avoid burnout and working all the time, but also keeping this really high bar and high expectations?
turns.zh: 当人们听到这句话时，他们可能会有的另一件事是，“天哪，我要花很多时间才能把它带到伊丽莎白满意的地方。”我知道你说过这并不一定意味着要花很多时间。对于如何避免倦怠和一直工作，同时保持如此高的标准和高期望，您有什么建议或想法吗？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: It truly is not about time. I even found myself in a meeting earlier today saying, "If we're clear on the objectives of something, it might be that the last 20% of polish on the document is a really bad use of time. So if we're going to come together to talk through..." Like quarterly business review was the example, what were the highlights? What were the low lights? What were the learnings from the quarter? Where are there places of misalignment? The reason we're doing the quarterly business review is to have a really candid conversation about how we think things are going, to have a debate about things where maybe we're stuck. It's not to have a perfectly polished document for that conversation. (00:26:08): So my feedback in that instance would be, I would much rather have someone spend the time thinking about what's the conversation we really want to have? "How do I tee that up?" Not, "Could I spend another 20 hours to make it look like everything's perfect in this document?" And so I think in that sense it's not just excellence, like you wrote the perfect document, I should probably be careful to not use that as the only example, but instead we really got to the outcome we wanted to get to because we were thoughtful about it and we put a lot of energy and time and iteration into making sure we got to that outcome.
turns.zh: 这确实不是时间的问题。我什至发现自己在今天早些时候的一次会议上说：“如果我们对某件事的目标很明确，那么对文档进行最后 20% 的润色可能是浪费时间。因此，如果我们要聚在一起讨论……”就像季度业务回顾就是一个例子，那么亮点是什么？昏暗的灯光是什么？本季度的经验教训是什么？哪些地方有错位的地方？我们进行季度业务审查的原因是要进行一次真正坦诚的对话，讨论我们对事情进展的看法，就我们可能陷入困境的事情进行辩论。这并不是为这次谈话准备一份完美的文件。 (00:26:08)：所以在这种情况下我的反馈是，我更希望有人花时间思考我们真正想要进行的对话是什么？ “我该怎么做呢？”不是“我可以再花 20 个小时让这份文档看起来一切都很完美吗？”所以我认为从这个意义上说，这不仅仅是卓越，就像你写了一份完美的文档一样，我可能应该小心不要用它作为唯一的例子，而是我们真正得到了我们想要得到的结果，因为我们对此进行了深思熟虑，我们投入了大量的精力、时间和迭代来确保我们得到这个结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is this an example where you gave someone feedback that they spent too much time on the polish or is this earlier? And to give the pyramid of this framework you kind of shared of set expectations, give specific feedback, help them fill the gap and then do it in private, is this the expectation setting in this example or is this feedback you spend too much time on this?
turns.zh: 这是一个你给某人反馈说他们花了太多时间在润色上的例子还是更早的？为了给这个框架的金字塔你分享设定的期望，提供具体的反馈，帮助他们填补空白，然后私下做，这是这个例子中的期望设置还是你在这个反馈上花了太多时间？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: This is expectation setting. So one of the things in my new role is that there's some practices that the team has had where they're trying to understand, Are we still going to have those practices? What's going to be the same versus different about those things?" and get an understanding of my expectations. So it's great that people ask that question so that I can be clear about, "Oh wait, if you're on the last 20% of this polishing the dock, I'd rather spend time over here. And here's how I would like the conversation to go so we all get something out of it instead of it feeling like it's just a leadership reviewer on my behalf." So in this specific situation, it was setting expectations ahead of time so that we can set everyone up for success.
turns.zh: 这是期望设定。因此，我的新角色中的一件事是，团队已经进行了一些实践，他们试图理解，我们还会有这些实践吗？这些事情有什么相同点和不同点？”并了解我的期望。所以很高兴人们问这个问题，这样我就可以清楚地知道，“哦等等，如果你在打磨码头的最后 20% 时间里，我宁愿花时间在这里。我希望对话能够这样进行，这样我们都能从中得到一些东西，而不是感觉这只是代表我的领导力审核员。”因此，在这种特定情况下，需要提前设定期望，以便我们可以为每个人的成功做好准备。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So we've kind of been talking around this, but this is an important part of the Netflix culture. Just broadly, Netflix has a really special and unique culture. Even though it's been around for I think over 25 years now, it feels like the culture has come up many times. There's that initial culture deck that came out that blew everyone's minds. There's a recent book, No Rules Rules I think it's called. And it feels like Netflix has done a great job at maintaining its culture. (00:28:10): It feels to me there's these three important elements, and maybe there's more. One is very high talent density and a focus on high performers. Two is candor and being really direct. And then three is giving people freedom and responsibility and getting rid of useless processes like vacation time and things like that. So maybe just to dive into that first one of high talent density and this focus on high performance. I guess the question there is just like, what does this look like in Netflix? And I imagine part of it is hiring, part of it is performance reviews. And then just why is it so important? Why is this such a focus on Netflix? What happens when you have such a high talent density?
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的。所以我们一直在讨论这个问题，但这是 Netflix 文化的重要组成部分。总的来说，Netflix 拥有非常特殊且独特的文化。尽管它已经存在了 25 年多了，但感觉这种文化已经出现过很多次了。最初的文化套牌的出现让每个人都大吃一惊。最近有一本书，我想它叫《无规则规则》。 Netflix 在维护其文化方面做得非常出色。 (00:28:10)：我觉得有这三个重要元素，也许还有更多。一是人才密度非常高，并且注重高绩效人才。二是坦诚和直接。第三是给予人们自由和责任，并摆脱诸如休假之类的无用流程。因此，也许只是深入探讨第一个高人才密度和对高绩效的关注。我想问题就在于，这在 Netflix 中是什么样子的？我想其中一部分是招聘，一部分是绩效评估。那么为什么它如此重要呢？为什么 Netflix 如此受关注？当人才密度如此之高时会发生什么？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: It's just so intrinsic to who Netflix is as a company. And in some ways it's very reflective of Reed Hastings as founder of Netflix. So when he founded Netflix and grew the company over time, it was with a belief that there could be a different approach to building a company that would make it a place that people thrived in and loved being and would feel different than other places, both in the quality of that talent density, but even more importantly, the excellence and the outcomes and that that's where people would derive a lot of sense of fulfillment. So it is very deeply seated at Netflix from its original days. (00:29:37): A big piece of that talent density is definitely hiring. So who are the people coming in and joining the team? But a lot of it is, we can't really have any of the other aspects of the culture, including candor, learning, seeking excellence and improvement, freedom and responsibility if you don't start with high talent density. (00:30:03): And so in some ways it's not the end, it's the means to the end in what Reed and the rest of the leadership team has been trying to build. And so in order to do that, you have to really hold yourself to a lot of stuff that doesn't feel like natural human behavior. What I mean by that is giving the feedback, this gets into the second bucket. So giving feedback, being candid around your expectations when they're not being met, what could be better in helping people improve, and be able to receive that type of feedback yourself in order to keep talent density high? Because no one comes to Netflix as a perfect human being and stays a perfect human being the whole time. We all have ways that we could grow and improve. And so in order to keep that bar high, you have to be willing to have those types of very uncomfortable conversations. It's an uncomfortable amount of candor and feedback in order to keep that bar high. (00:31:10): And then the other piece of it is another thing that doesn't come naturally to humans, which is making a call in pretty timely fashion if someone's not able to meet the bar, and to say either, "I don't think the role you're sitting in is the right role, or I don't think that Netflix is the right place for you," and to make that something that is part of best practice to get to a point where you could make that decision. And that's where we refer to the keepers test, which is really just a mental framing to make sure we hold ourselves accountable for this. Where if I'm asking myself the question, "If this person on my team came to me and said, 'I'm leaving today. I have a different opportunity and I would like to take it,' would I do everything I could to keep them at Netflix?" If not, then I should be having that tough conversation about, "Should you really be here? Are you in the right role?", if I might be a little bit relieved if you said you were leaving. (00:32:20): The reason the keeper test and that question is useful is because no one wants to think that way. It's very hard to say to someone, "I think this isn't the right fit. I think you should move on from the company." So we have to introduce some of those reflections in order to encourage the behavior. And we also then want to get to a place where when you're having that tough conversation, people aren't surprised by it. That is easier said than done. But you can only get to that conversation around, "I don't think Netflix and you are the right fit for one another" if you've been giving feedback along the way. And so it feels like in its most ideal state, it's a mutual observation. In practice, it's not always that smooth. Obviously we are humans. But that all feeds on itself in order to make sure that we're really holding ourselves to what we say our behavioral norms as part of the culture.
turns.zh: 这就是 Netflix 作为一家公司的本质。在某些方面，这非常反映了作为 Netflix 创始人的里德·黑斯廷斯 (Reed Hastings)。因此，当他创立 Netflix 并随着时间的推移不断发展公司时，他相信可以采用不同的方法来建立一家公司，使其成为一个让人们茁壮成长、热爱存在、感觉与其他地方不同的地方，无论是在人才密度的质量上，还是更重要的是，在卓越和成果上，人们会从中获得很多成就感。因此，从最初的时候起，它就在 Netflix 中根深蒂固。 (00:29:37)：人才密度的很大一部分肯定是招聘。那么谁是进来加入团队的人呢？但很多情况下，如果你不从高人才密度开始，我们就无法真正拥有这种文化的任何其他方面，包括坦诚、学习、追求卓越和改进、自由和责任。 (00:30:03)：所以从某些方面来说，这不是终点，而是里德和领导团队其他成员一直在努力建立的终点的手段。因此，为了做到这一点，你必须真正让自己坚持很多感觉不像人类自然行为的东西。我的意思是提供反馈，这属于第二个桶。因此，提供反馈，在未满足您的期望时坦诚地表达您的期望，还有什么比这更好地帮助人们改进，并且您自己能够收到此类反馈以保持高人才密度呢？因为没有人以一个完美的人的身份来到 Netflix 并一直保持一个完美的人。我们都有可以成长和进步的方法。因此，为了保持较高的标准，您必须愿意进行此类非常不舒服的对话。为了保持高标准，如此多的坦诚和反馈是令人不安的。 (00:31:10)：另一件事是人类不自然的事情，即如果有人无法达到标准，就会非常及时地打电话说，“我认为你所担任的角色不是正确的角色，或者我认为 Netflix 不适合你”，并将其作为最佳实践的一部分，以便你可以做出决定。这就是我们提到的守门员测试，这实际上只是一个心理框架，以确保我们对此负责。如果我问自己这样一个问题：“如果我团队中的这个人来找我说，‘我今天要离开。我有一个不同的机会，我想抓住它’，我会尽一切努力让他们留在 Netflix 吗？”如果不是，那么我应该进行一场艰难的对话，“你真的应该在这里吗？你的角色合适吗？”如果你说你要离开，我可能会稍微松一口气。 (00:32:20)：守门员测试和这个问题之所以有用，是因为没有人愿意这样想。很难对某人说：“我认为这不合适。我认为你应该离开公司。”因此，我们必须引入一些反思来鼓励这种行为。我们还希望达到这样一个境界：当你进行艰难的谈话时，人们不会对此感到惊讶。说起来容易做起来难。但如果您一直在提供反馈，那么您只能围绕“我认为 Netflix 和您不合适”进行对话。所以感觉就像在最理想的状态下，这是一种相互观察。实际上，事情并不总是那么顺利。显然我们是人类。但这一切都是为了确保我们真正遵守我们所说的作为文化一部分的行为规范。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How is that operationalized? Is that just mental model that you should have in mind? Or is it like every quarter you should go through this exercise? Is it part of the performance review process? How does that actually operationalize at Netflix?
turns.zh: 它是如何运作的？这只是您应该牢记的心理模型吗？或者是每个季度您都应该进行此练习吗？它是绩效评估流程的一部分吗？这在 Netflix 是如何实际运作的？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: It's definitely a mental model. So when we talk to managers about what does it mean to be a manager at Netflix, it would mean you should be with some frequency asking yourself this about the people on your team. People ask me frequently, "Am I passing your keeper test?" So it becomes part of a regular manager direct report, one on one. And it is just another way of saying, "Am I meeting your expectations? What's going well? What's not going well? How are you thinking about things?" And that can sometimes be a very awkward conversation to have. So in the middle of a lot of like, "We have to talk about this project or that deliverable or this thing that's happening," to take the time to step back and just say, "How am I doing?", can feel loaded sometimes. And the keeper test, while it feels like a very heavy concept, creates a lightness around being able to have that conversation regularly. So we do operationalize it. A point that you made, I'll just clarify, we don't have performance reviews.
turns.zh: 这绝对是一种心理模型。因此，当我们与经理谈论成为 Netflix 经理意味着什么时，这意味着您应该经常问自己关于团队成员的问题。人们经常问我：“我通过了你们的守门员测试吗？”因此，它成为定期经理直接报告的一部分，一对一。这只是另一种说法，“我达到你的期望了吗？什么进展顺利？什么进展不顺利？你对事情的看法如何？”有时这可能是一次非常尴尬的谈话。因此，在很多类似“我们必须谈论这个项目或可交付成果或正在发生的事情”的中间，花时间退一步说“我做得怎么样？”，有时会感到压力重重。守门员测试虽然感觉是一个非常沉重的概念，但围绕能够定期进行这种对话创造了一种轻松感。所以我们确实将其付诸实施。我只是澄清一下你提出的观点，我们没有绩效评估。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: So we don't have a practice that a lot of other companies do where we would think about reflecting on a rating of how things are going. We do have an annual cycle of 360 feedback where you request and receive feedback from a lot of people, but it's not an input to some output, it's just for the value of the feedback and to make sure we're keeping that muscle. And we have an annual compensation cycle where we reflect on how are people doing? And so you think about performance as part of both promotions and as part of compensation, but in that way it has to be part of the day-to-day and part of the operating rhythm because we don't create a process where that would come to the surface.
turns.zh: 因此，我们没有像许多其他公司那样考虑对事情进展情况进行评级的做法。我们确实有一个每年 360 度反馈的周期，您可以在其中请求并收到很多人的反馈，但这并不是某些输出的输入，这只是为了反馈的价值并确保我们保持这种实力。我们有一个年度薪酬周期，我们会反思人们的表现如何？因此，您可以将绩效视为促销和薪酬的一部分，但这样它就必须成为日常工作和运营节奏的一部分，因为我们不会创建一个将其浮现出来的流程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. I didn't know that. So the idea there is just ongoing, like the whole... So what many people dream of, no performance reviews, we'll give you ongoing real-time feedback. We don't have to wait six months. I feel like people talk about this but rarely do this, but that's how you guys operate.
turns.zh: 有趣的。我不知道。所以这个想法只是持续存在的，就像整个......所以很多人梦想的，没有绩效评估，我们会给你持续的实时反馈。我们不必等待六个月。我觉得人们谈论这个但很少这样做，但这就是你们的运作方式。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: In ideal.
turns.zh: 理想中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In ideal, yeah.
turns.zh: 理想情况下，是的。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: In practice. It's like you have to keep reminding yourself, "This is our ideal" because it's really easy to rely on the annual 360 cycle. And all of a sudden I do get about 300 pieces of feedback. And some of those things are on things that happened six months ago and I think, "Oh, I wish you had told me this at the time, that would've been more living the Netflix culture." So we have to push ourselves to do it that way. But yeah, that is if working well, it's very timely direct feedback. The 360 site goal is sort of the annual check-in on, "Let me get the full picture. Let me be able to distill some themes. Let me tee it up for a conversation with my manager." And then it does remove the sort of crutch of an every six month performance review or something like that.
turns.zh: 在实践中。就好像你必须不断提醒自己，“这是我们的理想”，因为每年 360 度的循环真的很容易依赖。突然间我确实收到了大约 300 条反馈。其中一些事情是六个月前发生的事情，我想，“哦，我希望你当时告诉我这些，那会让 Netflix 文化更加生动。”所以我们必须强迫自己这样做。但是，是的，如果运作良好，这是非常及时的直接反馈。 360 网站的目标有点像年度检查，“让我了解全貌。让我能够提炼出一些主题。让我准备好与我的经理进行对话。”然后它确实消除了每六个月进行一次绩效评估或类似的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you talked about this example of someone asking you often, "Am I meeting your keeper test?", it makes me feel like someone's just super nervous. They're like, "Am I passing your keeper test?" And it makes me feel like it could create a culture of just like a lot of stress and worry and this hunger games mentality of like, "I got to compete and worry and I might die or get fired any day." I'm guessing the solution to that is partly cultural. This is just the way we work. You don't need to stress all the time, but you may be let go if you're not meeting this keeper test. How do you avoid this just constant worry that you might be fired any day and that you may not be hitting the bar?
turns.zh: 当你谈到这个例子时，有人经常问你，“我符合你的守门员测试吗？”，这让我觉得有人超级紧张。他们就像是，“我通过了你们的守门员测试吗？”这让我觉得它可以创造一种充满压力和担忧的文化，以及这种饥饿游戏的心态，“我必须竞争并担心，我可能会死或有一天被解雇。”我猜解决这个问题的部分原因是文化。这就是我们的工作方式。你不需要一直有压力，但如果你没有达到这个守门员测试，你可能会被解雇。您如何避免这种不断担心自己可能有一天被解雇以及自己可能达不到标准的担忧？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: In my personal experience, I have felt a lot more at ease by having these conversations than by not having them. So in many roles I've had, I haven't been sure how I was doing or things I could be doing better on, and I didn't quite know how to get that information. And that made me feel much more stressed or nervous or at risk than having it be part of the culture to have those conversations. (00:37:45): So the thing that I think can be nerve wracking, and I feel it myself, is the high bar for excellence at Netflix and if we're doing this while you're surrounded by amazing people. And that can feed a sense of, "Am I doing well enough compared to how everyone else is doing? I know the bar's high." For the most part, that can drive people and in a good way, but in some ways it makes people nervous. And that's where I think it's helpful to know we expect to have these conversations so you can just kind of let your shoulders relax a little bit of, "Yes, the expectations are high, but my manager says I'm doing a great job, or my manager says I'm not doing a great job, but they gave me concrete things that I could do better." And so I think knowing is better than not. And so in that sense, it's the culture combined with the conversations around performance I hope take a little bit of that stress out of it. But I've certainly heard it a lot that without that conversation, people can be nervous.
turns.zh: 根据我个人的经验，进行这些对话比不进行这些对话让我感到轻松得多。因此，在我担任过的许多角色中，我不确定自己做得怎么样，或者哪些事情可以做得更好，而且我不太知道如何获取这些信息。与让这些对话成为文化的一部分相比，这让我感到更大的压力、紧张或风险。 (00:37:45)：因此，我认为最令人伤脑筋的事情（我自己也有这样的感觉）是 Netflix 追求卓越的高标准，如果我们在周围都是优秀的人的情况下这样做。这可以让人产生一种感觉：“与其他人相比，我做得足够好吗？我知道门槛很高。”在大多数情况下，这可以很好地激励人们，但在某些方面它会让人们感到紧张。这就是我认为知道我们期望进行这些对话是有帮助的，这样你就可以让你的肩膀放松一点，“是的，期望很高，但我的经理说我做得很好，或者我的经理说我做得不好，但他们给了我可以做得更好的具体事情。”所以我认为知道总比不知道好。因此，从这个意义上说，我希望文化与围绕绩效的对话相结合，可以减轻一点压力。但我确实经常听到这样的说法：如果没有这种对话，人们可能会感到紧张。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a good point and such a good example that I feel like every company wants to have a high bar and have only high performers and keep the bar really high for every person they hire. I'm curious, I know this could be its own podcast and book, but just in terms of hiring people that are amazing and keeping this bar of excellence, is there anything you can point out that might be helpful to other companies hiring to help identify amazing people and make sure that bar stays high? One thing I know is you guys pay a top market for salary. I think that's one unique thing about Netflix, is we just pay people. So maybe that's an part of this answer, but just what advice do you have for people to keep a really high bar in their talent?
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的观点和一个很好的例子，我觉得每个公司都希望有一个高标准，只拥有高绩效的员工，并为他们雇用的每个人保持很高的标准。我很好奇，我知道这可能是它自己的播客和书籍，但就雇用令人惊叹的人才并保持卓越标准而言，您是否可以指出任何可能对其他公司招聘人员有所帮助的内容，以帮助识别出色的人才并确保保持高标准？我知道的一件事是你们支付的薪水是最高市场水平的。我认为 Netflix 的独特之处在于我们只付钱给人们。所以也许这就是这个答案的一部分，但是你对人们保持高水平的才能有什么建议呢？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah, I mean on the compensation point, we pay what we call personal top of market, meaning we want to be highly competitive in the pay, but we don't want pay to be like the golden handcuffs of Netflix sets market rather than paying people a strongly competitive compensation. So I think that that's important for attracting and retaining talent and has been a big part of the culture, but almost more importantly, we hope we don't have to rely on that to want people to want to be at Netflix or for us to be able to assess whether people are going to thrive at Netflix. (00:40:20): The way that I've thought about hiring with that context is we know we're going to offer you very highly competitive compensation, but are you going to come to Netflix and help us identify the right problems to solve or new ways to solve existing problems? And that's a different way of hiring than you might think about, especially at scale where you're saying, "Does this person have this skill, this skill, this skill? Check they're going to fit in this box and they're going to deliver this work that I need them to do." I'm being intentionally simplistic. I recognize a lot of people don't hire actually that way. But at Netflix we try really hard to say we're looking for the new perspective or the person who's actually going to make us stronger as a team. So thinking about additive skills, additive perspectives, people who are going to push our thinking on something. That tends to help us with thinking about talent density because you're constantly introducing people to the team who uplevel. (00:41:25): So then the questions you have to ask in an interview might be different because yes, we're trying to assess do you have the baseline skills to be successful here, but we're also looking for the things that make people exceptional or even stronger than the team we've got. And then you think about making the magical teams comprised of all those amazing minds and what can you get out of that. And that feels like more that the talent density and practice.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是在薪酬方面，我们支付的是所谓的个人市场最高水平，这意味着我们希望在薪酬方面具有高度竞争力，但我们不希望薪酬像Netflix设定的金手铐那样设定市场，而不是向人们支付极具竞争力的薪酬。因此，我认为这对于吸引和留住人才非常重要，并且一直是公司文化的重要组成部分，但更重要的是，我们希望不必依赖这一点来希望人们愿意加入 Netflix，或者让我们能够评估人们是否会在 Netflix 茁壮成长。 (00:40:20)：在这种情况下，我考虑招聘的方式是，我们知道我们将为您提供极具竞争力的薪酬，但您是否会来 Netflix 帮助我们确定需要解决的正确问题或解决现有问题的新方法？这是一种与你想象的不同的招聘方式，尤其是在规模上，你会说，“这个人有这个技能，这个技能，这个技能吗？检查一下他们是否适合这个框，他们是否能够完成我需要他们做的工作。”我是故意简单化的。我认识到很多人实际上并不是这样招聘的。但在 Netflix，我们非常努力地宣称我们正在寻找新的视角或真正能让我们作为一个团队变得更强大的人。因此，要考虑附加技能、附加观点以及将推动我们思考某件事的人。这往往有助于我们思考人才密度，因为你不断地向团队介绍升级的人。 (00:41:25)：那么你在面试中要问的问题可能会有所不同，因为是的，我们正在尝试评估你是否具备在这里取得成功的基本技能，但我们也在寻找使人们脱颖而出甚至比我们现有团队更强大的东西。然后你会考虑让所有这些令人惊叹的人才组成神奇的团队，以及你能从中得到什么。这感觉更像是人才密度和实践。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So the advice there essentially is, don't look for someone just simply great. Look for someone that raises the bar for the whole team, brings in a whole new perspective.
turns.zh: 知道了。所以这里的建议本质上是，不要仅仅寻找优秀的人。寻找能够提高整个团队的标准、带来全新视角的人。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yes. That's a great way to say it. Yeah, it's a good way to say it.
turns.zh: 是的。这是一个很好的表达方式。是的，这是一个很好的表达方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think what's great about this idea of just maintaining excellence consistently is that the best people want to work with the best people. And as soon as there's one person that sucks and the company allows for that, it just brings everyone down because they know, "Hey, we can be okay. We'll stick or no one's going to do anything about it." And when you make it clear, we only want the best and only hire the best and only keep the best, it keeps the best there, right? I imagine that's part of the strategy.
turns.zh: 我认为持续保持卓越这一理念的伟大之处在于，最优秀的人愿意与最优秀的人一起工作。一旦有人表现得很糟糕，而公司允许这种情况发生，就会让每个人都很沮丧，因为他们知道，“嘿，我们可以没事的。我们会坚持下去，否则没有人会采取任何行动。”当你说清楚时，我们只想要最好的，只雇用最好的，只保留最好的，这样就留住了最好的，对吧？我想这是战略的一部分。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah. It's definitely the goal. And I think understanding that having gaps in the team and people's skillsets or their behavior can be really toxic for other people on the team. So it's a cost.
turns.zh: 是的。这绝对是目标。我认为，团队和人们的技能或行为之间的差距可能会对团队中的其他人造成真正的伤害。所以这是一个成本。
