turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: That is freedom and responsibility in a nutshell. So let me explain that. It's a good question. It's kind of related to what I was saying earlier, that talent density is a prerequisite for a lot of the other ways we operate. So if we want to create a work environment where we are not prescriptive about how people solve problems or the scope of problems that they could tackle, assuming they're highly impactful for the business, and we don't have a lot of process around that work, so think about being able to make large innovations to our engineering systems or introducing new ways to think about metrics and experimentation, we get a lot of those things because we give people the freedom and the space to explore and question things and experiment in a way with solutions. I think that that would be very hard if not dangerous if we didn't have a high talent density. (00:45:32): It's really not a top down do A, then B, then C. Even in how we go through some of our planning processes or thinking about how we think about priorities, there is a lot of room for contribution across all levels of the team and that requires talent density. And then there's things like you have to have amazing people if you're not going to have really strict guardrails that would influence the consumer experience or business stakeholders experience. We do give people a lot of responsibility on those things. So I think the lack of process and prescriptiveness is all hinging on we've got amazing people who are smart, but even better have strong judgment.
turns.zh: 简而言之，这就是自由和责任。让我解释一下。这是一个好问题。这与我之前所说的有点相关，人才密度是我们许多其他运营方式的先决条件。因此，如果我们想要创建一个工作环境，在这个环境中，我们不规定人们如何解决问题或他们可以解决的问题范围，假设这些问题对业务有很大影响，而且我们没有太多围绕这项工作的流程，所以考虑能够对我们的工程系统进行重大创新或引入新的方式来思考指标和实验，我们会得到很多这样的东西，因为我们给了人们自由和空间来探索和质疑事物并以解决方案的方式进行实验。我认为，如果我们没有高人才密度，那即使不是危险，也会非常困难。 (00:45:32)：这确实不是自上而下先做 A，然后是 B，然后是 C。即使在我们如何进行一些规划流程或考虑如何考虑优先级方面，团队的各个级别都有很大的贡献空间，这需要人才密度。然后，如果你不打算有真正严格的护栏来影响消费者体验或业务利益相关者的体验，那么你就必须拥有出色的人才。我们确实在这些事情上赋予人们很多责任。因此，我认为流程和规范性的缺乏完全取决于我们拥有出色的人才，他们很聪明，但更好的是拥有强大的判断力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is kind of what you always hear from people giving founders advice is, "Just hire amazing people, get out of their way and let them do their job," which is often not a successful experience. What are examples that either things that came out of this freedom, I don't know, products or features or ideas that came out of this or policies or processes you don't have that everyone else might have? So I know there's no vacation time, there's unlimited vacation time, I assume. Is that still a thing? Unlimited vacation time?
turns.zh: 你经常从给创始人建议的人那里听到这样的话：“只要雇佣优秀的人，别妨碍他们，让他们做好自己的工作”，这通常不是一个成功的经历。有哪些例子可以说明这种自由带来的东西（我不知道）、由此产生的产品、功能或想法，或者你没有但其他人可能有的政策或流程？所以我知道没有假期，我想假期时间是无限的。那还是一件事吗？休假时间无限？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. All right, great. And I know performance reviews, you talked about that. So I guess in either direction, is there an example of something that came out of this freedom or some process that which surprised people that you don't have or a framework or system?
turns.zh: 好吧，酷。好吧，太好了。我知道绩效评估，你也谈到了这一点。所以我想无论是哪个方向，是否有一个来自这种自由的例子，或者一些让人们感到惊讶的过程，或者一个框架或系统？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: We've been able to deliver... I'll speak to my own team around innovations in our content delivery network or innovations in encoding or innovations in discovery and personalization. We're not driven by some leader saying, "I think this is a priority." They were driven in many cases by individual contributors who had great ideas for innovation. So a lot of the stuff that Netflix has succeeded in, came from creating space for people on the team. So there's probably thousands of examples of product features and things like that that came out of creating this space. And right now, the trick is finding the sweet spot so that we can operate efficiently at this type of scale without snuffing out some of that, what was kind of the core beauty of the culture.
turns.zh: 我们已经能够交付......我将与我自己的团队讨论我们的内容交付网络的创新或编码的创新或发现和个性化的创新。我们并不是被某些领导人所说的“我认为这是一个优先事项”所驱使。在许多情况下，它们是由具有伟大创新想法的个人贡献者推动的。因此，Netflix 的很多成功都来自于为团队成员创造空间。因此，创建这个空间时可能会产生数千个产品功能和类似内容的示例。现在，关键是找到最佳点，以便我们能够在这种规模下高效运营，而不会扼杀一些文化的核心之美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe a last question around just the culture. We talked about candor a bit. I'm just curious if there's an example that comes to mind of an example of candor that you recently saw or had to be the candid person that might be interesting to share where it's like, "Oh wow, that's what you mean when you say a culture of candor."
turns.zh: 也许最后一个问题只是关于文化。我们谈了一些坦诚的话题。我只是很好奇，是否有一个你最近看到的坦率的例子，或者必须是一个坦率的人，可能会很有趣地分享，“哦，哇，这就是你所说的坦率文化的意思。”

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: There's a couple things that come to mind. I am generally a transparent leader, meaning I share information freely and openly. It's part of the culture to context, not control, which means part of my job is to make sure that people have the context they need to do their jobs well. And in practice, that means I take notes in leadership meetings and I share those notes with the whole organization. And that is sometimes it includes candor around reflections on things that aren't going well or problems we need to solve. Sometimes it's just letting people know, "Here's what leadership's talking about so that they have a sense of what's top of mind." But it's a version of transparency that I feel strongly about, doesn't exist a lot of other places. I think it's a version of candor too in being able to share... I can't always share every detail of everything that we're talking about, but I do try to share things that probably push the boundary a little bit in the team, feeling like they understand what's happening across the company and what I'm thinking about. (00:49:22): And then there's a second example that comes to mind, which is, until two years ago, individual contributors didn't have levels at Netflix. So all engineers were just senior engineers, all data scientists were senior data scientists, and we did not have a leveling system. We introduced IC levels two years ago almost exactly. And it was a big, big, big shift because it was seen as something that was sort of sacred of it. A lot of people came to Netflix because we didn't have it. We didn't have process around promotions. This is probably part of why we never had performance reviews, because promotions really weren't at play. And it gave people a sense of freedom of not having to worry about that type of structure. But when you get to a scale of an organization, we needed some type of scaffolding to say, "We want to talk about how we compose teams. When do we need the person who has 30 years of experience? When do we want to have a new grad?" Because that's what the work requires. We didn't have a language for it. (00:50:27): So I introduced Levels a couple of years ago and we had quite a change rollercoaster is the only way I can describe how it went.
turns.zh: 我想到了几件事。我通常是一个透明的领导者，这意味着我自由、公开地分享信息。这是环境文化的一部分，而不是控制，这意味着我工作的一部分是确保人们拥有做好工作所需的环境。在实践中，这意味着我在领导会议上做笔记，并与整个组织分享这些笔记。有时它包括对进展不顺利的事情或我们需要解决的问题进行坦率的反思。有时只是让人们知道，“这是领导层正在谈论的内容，以便他们了解最重要的事情。”但这是我强烈感受到的一种透明度，在很多其他地方并不存在。我认为这也是一种能够分享的坦诚……我不能总是分享我们正在谈论的所有细节，但我确实尝试分享可能会在团队中稍微突破界限的事情，感觉他们了解整个公司正在发生的事情以及我在想什么。 (00:49:22)：然后我想到了第二个例子，那就是，直到两年前，个人贡献者在 Netflix 还没有级别。所以所有工程师都只是高级工程师，所有数据科学家都是高级数据科学家，我们没有分级系统。我们在两年前几乎一模一样地推出了 IC 级别。这是一个很大很大的转变，因为它被视为某种神圣的东西。很多人来观看 Netflix 是因为我们没有它。我们没有促销流程。这可能是我们从未进行绩效评估的部分原因，因为晋升确实没有发挥作用。它给人一种不必担心那种结构的自由感。但是，当你达到一定规模的组织时，我们需要某种类型的脚手架来说：“我们想讨论如何组成团队。我们什么时候需要拥有 30 年经验的人？我们什么时候想要新毕业生？”因为这就是工作所需要的。我们没有语言来表达它。 (00:50:27)：所以几年前我引入了关卡，我们发生了很大的变化，过山车是我可以描述它是如何进行的唯一方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a good phrase.
turns.zh: 这句话说得好。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah, it was sort of like being the tumble dry machine for a few months, and so really talking through it with the team. That's just context and backdrop. For an example of candor recently, which is, we had kind of a postmortem or a retro on how has it gone with IC levels. So it's kind of like wells, not wells. And I would normally think in a lot of cultures it would be like, "Well, we got past that change. We're living that change." Don't reflect on it. Because that kind of opened some of that early debate. And I felt differently about it. I think it's a good example of being candid about, this was a big change for us. It hasn't all gone perfectly. There's a lot that we can do better in how we implement levels at Netflix. And I would rather share that information than pretend it's all gone swimmingly and we achieved every objective. So I think that I try to build examples like that because I do think that level of candor and reflection helps build the sense of community and trust across the team.
turns.zh: 是的，这有点像几个月的滚筒烘干机，因此与团队进行了真正的讨论。这只是背景和背景。举个最近坦率的例子，我们对 IC 水平的变化进行了事后分析或回顾。所以它有点像井，而不是井。我通常会认为在很多文化中都会这样，“好吧，我们已经过去了这种变化。我们正在经历这种变化。”不要反思它。因为这引发了一些早期的争论。我对此有不同的感受。我认为这是一个坦诚的好例子，这对我们来说是一个很大的变化。一切还没有那么完美。在 Netflix 的关卡实现方式上，我们还有很多可以做得更好的地方。我宁愿分享这些信息，也不愿假装一切进展顺利，我们实现了每一个目标。所以我认为我尝试建立这样的例子是因为我确实认为坦诚和反思的程度有助于在整个团队中建立社区意识和信任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome example. Kind of along the lines of that, but also this category of freedom and responsibility, something Netflix innovated long ago, and I'm curious if this is still a thing, is this idea of Chaos Monkeys, which essentially are a program that runs on your infrastructure that just kills random processes and things and just to see what breaks and make sure things are stable when things actually start falling apart. Is Chaos Monkeys... Was that what it's called? And then is that still a thing? Is there still some Chaos Monkeys running around the servers?
turns.zh: 这是一个很棒的例子。类似的，还有这种自由和责任的类别，Netflix 很久以前就创新了，我很好奇这是否仍然是一个东西，这就是 Chaos Monkeys 的想法，它本质上是一个在你的基础设施上运行的程序，它只是杀死随机的进程和事物，只是为了看看什么出了问题，并确保当事物真正开始崩溃时事物是稳定的。混沌猴子……是这个名字吗？那么这仍然是一件事吗？服务器周围是否还有一些混沌猴子在运行？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Not unbridled Chaos Monkeys. No.
turns.zh: 不是肆无忌惮的混沌猴子。不。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Contains chaos and niche.
turns.zh: 好的。包含混乱和利基。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Bur no, we carry too much responsibility, speaking of freedom and responsibility for the member experience to inject pain, though we do do a lot of experiments to test resilience, and that does probably mean injecting things that we're not quite sure whether A is better than B. And so that happens across engineering systems really at scale. But it is not for pure chaos, it's for intentional learning and so we can avoid making bigger mistakes. And then as we go into new efforts like cloud games, we have a beta that's out now, Live would be another example. We do try to come up with intentionally low profile examples where we can test the bounds of our systems in a way that's unlikely to damage the member experience. But that's less randomness, more by design. And so we're doing that in a few places that feels mostly good engineering practice so we can understand when it's really showtime and we're going to really test our systems, will they be able to perform like we want them to.
turns.zh: 但不，我们承担了太多的责任，说到自由和责任，让成员体验注入痛苦，尽管我们确实做了很多实验来测试弹性，这可能意味着注入我们不太确定 A 是否比 B 更好的东西。所以这种情况在整个工程系统中确实大规模发生。但这并不是为了纯粹的混乱，而是为了有意识的学习，这样我们就可以避免犯更大的错误。然后，当我们开展云游戏等新工作时，我们现在已经推出了测试版，Live 将是另一个例子。我们确实尝试提出故意低调的示例，以便我们可以以不太可能损害会员体验的方式测试我们系统的边界。但这并不是随机性，更多的是设计。因此，我们在一些感觉良好的工程实践的地方这样做，这样我们就可以了解何时真正展示，我们将真正测试我们的系统，它们是否能够像我们希望的那样运行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: RIP Chaos Monkey.
turns.zh: 安息吧混沌猴子。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So kind of along these lines of data, so data itself has always been at the heart of Netflix. My understanding is the way the data team and the insights team is structured has been one of the reasons Netflix has been so successful. And that's the team you led before you moved into this new role. Can you just talk about how these teams are structured and why this structure is so effective?
turns.zh: 正是沿着这些数据思路，数据本身一直是 Netflix 的核心。我的理解是，数据团队和洞察团队的构建方式是 Netflix 如此成功的原因之一。这就是您担任新职位之前所领导的团队。您能否谈谈这些团队的结构以及为什么这种结构如此有效？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah. I certainly like to think of it as being special. It's unusual. I can explain why. So the scale of company that Netflix now is very often data oriented teams are embedded in other parts of the business. So it could either be they're embedded in a business line like ads or games, or they are organized more functionally separating data engineers from data scientists, from analytics engineers, from consumer researchers. We've resisted that and kept a centralized team that is both functionally diverse. So across all those types of functions that I just described and works on nearly every area of the business from within the team. I sort of understand why a lot of companies move away from this because it really does require basically extraordinary partnership that we would have people working on data problems that don't report into the teams that are relying on them. (00:55:30): But the benefit we get is we get to think about our functional expertise. So are we really world's best data engineers, world's best data scientists? And how do we continue to be ever better from a functional and technical perspective? It gives people better career paths because there's more mobility across the teams. It feels like a team that has a functional expertise with a lot of different problems to solve. And so I think it enables more cross-pollination of ideas in a way. (00:56:03): It also allows us to be really objective. That is probably the most important thing, that our job is not to tell the story that someone wants to hear with the data or to solve the problem that someone thinks is most important. It's for us to have our own perspective about things. I think that that uplevels the whole organization because it means that we're able to be truth tellers or to be curious in a way that might not fit if we had a different organizational structure. We have to balance, that would be a good partner, deliver on the things we agreed were priorities, be flexible with how we're spending our time, but it gives us agency and responsibility beyond that. And I feel like the team takes that very seriously. So I've seen examples of that in how we bring data to a lot of spaces, including how we partner with engineering on data-related topics or how we partner with content that I'm not sure we would've gotten to if not for having that kernel that's sort of a center of excellence around it.
turns.zh: 是的。我当然喜欢认为它很特别。这很不寻常。我可以解释为什么。因此，Netflix 现在的公司规模往往是以数据为导向的团队嵌入到业务的其他部分。因此，它们要么嵌入到广告或游戏等业务线中，要么在功能上将数据工程师与数据科学家、分析工程师和消费者研究人员分开。我们抵制了这一点，并保留了一个功能多样化的集中团队。因此，我刚刚描述的所有这些类型的职能都适用于团队内部几乎每个业务领域。我有点理解为什么很多公司放弃了这一点，因为它确实需要基本上非凡的合作伙伴关系，我们会让人们处理数据问题，而不向依赖他们的团队报告。 (00:55:30)：但我们得到的好处是我们可以考虑我们的职能专业知识。那么我们真的是世界上最好的数据工程师、世界上最好的数据科学家吗？从功能和技术角度来看，我们如何继续变得更好？它为人们提供了更好的职业道路，因为团队之间的流动性更大。感觉就像一个拥有职能专业知识、需要解决许多不同问题的团队。所以我认为它在某种程度上可以实现更多的思想交叉授粉。 (00:56:03)：这也让我们能够真正客观。这可能是最重要的事情，我们的工作不是用数据讲述某人想听的故事，也不是解决某人认为最重要的问题。我们对事物有自己的看法。我认为这提高了整个组织的水平，因为这意味着我们能够成为说真话的人，或者以一种如果我们有不同的组织结构则可能不适合的方式保持好奇心。我们必须保持平衡，这将是一个很好的合作伙伴，交付我们同意的优先事项，灵活地安排我们的时间，但它给了我们除此之外的代理权和责任。我觉得团队非常重视这一点。因此，我看到过这样的例子：我们如何将数据带到很多空间，包括我们如何与数据相关主题的工程合作，或者我们如何与内容合作，如果没有那个围绕它的卓越中心的内核，我不确定我们是否会得到这些内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's Data and Insights, that was the team that you ran. Insights, is that describing user research or what does that have function actually?
turns.zh: 这是数据和洞察，这就是您管理的团队。见解，这是描述用户研究还是实际上有什么作用？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: So part of Data and Insights is a Consumer Insights team that includes a lot of different flavors of research really. So in some ways, consumer is even a misnomer because there's parts of the team that do internal research, for example, on tools and products for our studio productions. So that's more of a user research-oriented versus consumer. And then the parts of that team that are consumer-oriented do things all the way from content screenings to make titles the best version of themselves before they're on the service to more traditional UX research to think about how can we deliver the best title discovery experience or how can we think about things that improve accessibility? And then that team has a global remit. So there's also teams that are more local or regional expertise in understanding consumer needs and entertainment. (00:57:12): So Consumer Insights and a team, formerly known as still kind of known as a shorthand, data science and engineering, combined together to create data and insights probably about two years ago. That's another piece that's unusual. It becomes truly a full-stack data and research expertise. And so we could tackle a problem like, what's the right way to think about recommendations and how best to surface them in a way that combines attitudinal research, qualitative and quantitative with behavioral research on more of the data science, data engineering analytics side.
turns.zh: 因此，数据和洞察部门的一部分是消费者洞察团队，其中确实包括许多不同风格的研究。因此，在某些方面，“消费者”甚至是一个用词不当，因为团队的某些部分正在进行内部研究，例如，对我们工作室制作的工具和产品进行研究。因此，这更多的是面向用户研究而不是面向消费者。然后，该团队中以消费者为导向的部分会做各种事情，从内容筛选到使游戏本身成为最好的版本，然后再提供服务，再到更传统的用户体验研究，思考我们如何才能提供最佳的游戏发现体验，或者我们如何考虑提高可访问性的事情？然后该团队的职责是全球性的。因此，还有一些团队在了解消费者需求和娱乐方面更具本地或区域专业知识。 (00:57:12)：大约两年前，消费者洞察和一个团队（以前称为数据科学和工程）结合在一起创建了数据和见解。这是另一件不寻常的作品。它成为真正的全栈数据和研究专业知识。因此，我们可以解决这样的问题：思考建议的正确方法是什么，以及如何最好地以将态度研究、定性和定量与更多数据科学、数据工程分析方面的行为研究相结合的方式呈现它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's super cool because I think it's really rare that what people think of user research is within the data org. And I think that might be a solution to some of the backlash a lot of user research teams get where they're like, I don't know, what are you guys doing all this anecdotal evidence if it's under the same org. I feel like that leads to a lot more credibility and avoids this like, "Oh, data's telling me this thing. This user research team is telling me this thing. What should we do?"
turns.zh: 这非常酷，因为我认为人们对用户研究的看法很少发生在数据组织内部。我认为这可能是解决许多用户研究团队遇到的一些强烈反对的方法，他们会说，我不知道，如果这些轶事证据是在同一个组织下，你们在做什么。我觉得这会带来更多的可信度，并避免这样的情况，“哦，数据告诉我这件事。这个用户研究团队告诉我这件事。我们应该做什么？”

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, Consumer Insights is one of the newer teams for me; it wasn't in my background to lead a team like that and not in my individual training, but they are critical for making sure we keep a consumer orientation, a member orientation on things. I have loved to watch the teams collaborate on problems because we talk about it as a superpower internally in combining those skill sets. So I think the Consumer Insights team at Netflix has had a lot of credibility in a certain area of expertise and we took it to the next level by combining it with other functional expertise. So it's not required in every problem space. So we try not to overdo it and say we need to be collaborating everywhere because that just feels like the wrong expectation, but we try to make the most of it in spaces where we really benefit. So yeah, it's worked out really well.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是，消费者洞察对我来说是较新的团队之一；我的背景不是领导这样的团队，也不是我的个人培训，但它们对于确保我们保持消费者导向、会员导向至关重要。我喜欢看到团队合作解决问题，因为我们在内部将其视为结合这些技能的超级力量。因此，我认为 Netflix 的消费者洞察团队在某个专业领域拥有很高的可信度，我们通过将其与其他职能专业知识相结合，将其提升到了一个新的水平。所以并不是每个问题空间都需要它。因此，我们尽量不要做得太过分，并说我们需要在各地进行合作，因为这感觉像是错误的期望，但我们试图在我们真正受益的领域充分利用它。是的，效果非常好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. I want to ask two more questions before we get to our very exciting lightning around. And they're both skills that [inaudible 01:00:08] have told me you're very good at. One is that you are very intentional and thoughtful about staying close to individual teams and individuals within the company, even though you're higher and higher in the org. I'm curious how you do that, how you actually practice this skill of staying really close to teams at the bottom of the ladder and individuals that are working on things on the ground basically?
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的。在我们开始讨论令人兴奋的闪电之前，我想再问两个问题。 [听不清 01:00:08] 告诉我你非常擅长这两项技能。一是你非常有意和深思熟虑地与公司内的各个团队和个人保持密切联系，即使你在组织中的职位越来越高。我很好奇你是如何做到这一点的，你是如何实际练习这种与底层团队和基本上在实地工作的个人保持密切联系的技能的？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: A lot of it is how I spend my time and fighting to preserve opportunities to connect with people. So examples would be, I still have biweekly office hours, people sign up for slots. It can feel a little like speed dating for 20 minute slots, but I get to meet a whole bunch of people and hear about work, hear what's top of mind. People book them out many months ahead and it's just an opportunity to stay in touch. And then I do Ask Me Anything sessions with teams of different sizes depending on how intimate we want it to feel, but truly anything is fair game as a way to get to know me as a person, for me to hear questions, to try to be candid about what I can answer or can't answer. And so those things have helped me maintain connection, but both of those examples are about making the time for it. (01:01:50): So what I have found as my role has changed is that it just wouldn't happen if I didn't make it a priority. And then through those types of sessions, I do think I become or I hope to become more approachable so people know, "You can send me a Slack message, you can send me an email. Like I mentioned earlier, I'm going to respond to you as quickly as I can because I want to hold myself to that bar." And so that builds a flow of communication between me and the team that I really value... I don't think I would want to do my job if I didn't have those points of connection, so that helps too.
turns.zh: 其中很大一部分是我如何度过时间并努力保留与人交往的机会。例子是，我仍然有每两周一次的办公时间，人们报名参加空档。这感觉有点像 20 分钟的快速约会，但我可以见到很多人，了解工作情况，了解最重要的事情。人们提前几个月就预订了，这只是一个保持联系的机会。然后我会与不同规模的团队进行“有问必答”会议，具体取决于我们希望感觉有多亲密，但实际上，任何事情都是公平的游戏，可以作为了解我这个人的一种方式，让我听到问题，尝试坦诚地回答我能回答或不能回答的问题。所以这些事情帮助我保持联系，但这两个例子都是为了腾出时间。 (01:01:50)：因此，随着我的角色发生变化，我发现如果我不将其作为优先事项，这种情况就不会发生。然后通过这些类型的会议，我确实认为我变得或者我希望变得更加平易近人，这样人们就知道，“你可以给我发一条 Slack 消息，你可以给我发一封电子邮件。就像我之前提到的，我会尽快回复你，因为我想把自己控制在这个标准上。”这样就在我和我真正重视的团队之间建立了沟通流程……如果我没有这些联系点，我想我就不会想做我的工作，所以这也有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you also send that email to everyone after every leadership meeting, so they're like, "Oh yeah, Elizabeth."
turns.zh: 每次领导会议后，你都会向每个人发送该电子邮件，所以他们会说，“哦，是的，伊丽莎白。”

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah, they hear from me. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，他们收到我的来信。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind of related to this, so we have a mutual friend, that's how we got connected. Ali Rao, she was a data scientist at Airbnb, now she's at Uber. She had a question that she wanted me to ask, and it's about how good you are at being present. So her question is something she's noticed about. "Something I've noticed about her is how 100% present she is no matter who she talks to. Do you have any advice for people to get better at this? Because it's so hard in the day of email and iPhones and Slack." Her questions like, "When does she respond to stuff if not sometimes in meetings?"
turns.zh: 与此有点相关，所以我们有一个共同的朋友，这就是我们的联系方式。 Ali Rao，她曾是 Airbnb 的数据科学家，现在在 Uber 工作。她有一个问题要我问，是关于你在场的表现如何。所以她的问题是她注意到的。 “我注意到她的一个特点是，无论与谁交谈，她都百分百在场。你对人们在这方面做得更好有什么建议吗？因为在电子邮件、iPhone 和 Slack 的时代，这太难了。”她的问题包括：“如果有时在会议上不回应，她什么时候回应？”

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: I actually think I'm the most present when I'm having conversations like this one. I do preserve a lot of time to have one-on-one conversations where I'm genuinely curious about how someone's doing, how I can help them, what they're excited about that's authentic. And so while my EA would probably cringe at saying I like to spend time doing a lot of those one-on-ones, it is relatively easier for me to say the human connection is part of what I enjoy about this. I think that's true for a lot of people in what we get out of work and life, but I try to live that in those meetings. I'm probably not as good when we're talking about meetings of 30 people and I'm multitasking, so I'll admit to doing that for sure. But I think the one-on-one conversations I treat as being pretty sacred. (01:04:09): One of the things I've noticed that helps me continue to invest in that and maybe is helpful for other people is some of my greatest friends and connections, including people like Ali, are people I met along the way professionally. So I worked very closely with Ally's husband, Keith Henwood, at multiple places, both Analysis Group and at Lyft. And that means that it's created opportunities and it's been points of connection. And so you get back what you give basically. (01:04:45): There are people in my life who are part of my life because I worked with them or because I crossed paths. And I like to think that if I can make a positive mark on them, it'll come back and be at some point too. So I think to distill that is that I truly enjoy it. It's what I get out of especially work. And then it's my community. And that's served me really well over time. And so I have given people advice of, "This is a small community, think about what you're investing in other people because that will matter down the line for yourself too" and I try to live that myself.
turns.zh: 事实上，我认为当我进行这样的对话时，我是最在场的。我确实会留出很多时间进行一对一的对话，我真诚地好奇某人在做什么，我如何帮助他们，他们对什么是真实的感到兴奋。因此，虽然我的 EA 可能会不好意思说我喜欢花时间进行大量的一对一交流，但对我来说，相对更容易说人际关系是我喜欢这样做的一部分。我认为对于很多人来说，我们从工作和生活中得到的都是如此，但我试图在这些会议中体现这一点。当我们谈论 30 人的会议时，我可能不太擅长，而且我要同时处理多项任务，所以我承认我确实会这样做。但我认为一对一的谈话是非常神圣的。 (01:04:09)：我注意到的一件事可以帮助我继续投资，也许对其他人也有帮助，那就是我一些最好的朋友和人脉，包括像阿里这样的人，都是我在职业生涯中遇到的人。因此，我在 Analysis Group 和 Lyft 等多个地方与艾莉的丈夫基思·亨伍德 (Keith Henwood) 密切合作。这意味着它创造了机会并且成为了联系点。所以你基本上会得到你所付出的东西。 (01:04:45)：我生命中有些人因为我与他们一起工作或者因为我有过交集而成为我生活的一部分。我喜欢认为，如果我能给他们留下积极的印象，它也会在某个时候回来。所以我认为提炼出它是我真正喜欢的。这是我从特别工作中得到的。然后是我的社区。随着时间的推移，这对我很有帮助。所以我给人们的建议是，“这是一个小社区，想想你在其他人身上投资了什么，因为这对你自己也很重要”，我自己也努力实践这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's such good advice. There's kind of two things that come to mind there. One is treat people the way you want to be treated. Someone once said that maybe. And I think you've come back to this a couple times, this idea of just pay attention to what gives you energy and that you're good at and just almost double down on that. Just make that more and more of a superpower.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一个很好的建议。我想到了两件事。一是你愿意人怎样待你，你也要怎样待人。有人曾经说过，也许吧。我想你已经回到这个话题好几次了，这个想法就是关注那些给你能量的东西，以及你擅长的东西，并且几乎要加倍努力。只是让它越来越成为一个超级大国。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Yeah, that last part resonates. It's been a big part of my personal and professional practice to reflect on how I'm feeling, what I'm excited about, what I'm enjoying. I do think it helps me be more grounded, which maybe helps me be more present or helps me be a better manager or leader. That might be part of the secret sauce too, but it is part of my practice.
turns.zh: 是的，最后一部分引起了共鸣。反思我的感受、我对什么感到兴奋、我喜欢什么，是我个人和职业实践的重要组成部分。我确实认为这可以帮助我更加脚踏实地，这也许可以帮助我更加活在当下，或者帮助我成为一名更好的经理或领导者。这也可能是秘密武器的一部分，但它是我实践的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can't help but ask, is this an actual practice? Do you do this on a regular basis or is this just something you think about like, "I should reflect back"?
turns.zh: 我不禁要问，这是实际的做法吗？您是否定期这样做，或者这只是您的想法，例如“我应该反思”？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: I wish I was so advanced to say I meditate and I create all this structure. It's more that I think I mentioned maybe I'm an introvert, so I do spend some time alone. That's how I recharge. And early mornings, especially people who know me sometimes are horrified at the time of day I send emails, but early mornings are a quiet time for me where I do try to have a daily check-in of just how are things going, why am I feeling anxious, why am I feeling excited. And it's kind of a muscle you build. So while I don't write in a journal, I don't have a meditation practice, I do have a time of day when I try to keep it protected from other things so that I can think for a second.
turns.zh: 我希望我能如此先进地说我冥想并创造了所有这些结构。我想我提到的更多的是，也许我是一个内向的人，所以我确实花了一些时间独处。这就是我充电的方式。清晨，尤其是认识我的人有时会对我发送电子邮件的时间感到恐惧，但清晨对我来说是一个安静的时间，我每天都会尝试检查事情进展如何，为什么我感到焦虑，为什么我感到兴奋。这是你锻炼的肌肉。因此，虽然我不写日记，也没有进行冥想练习，但我确实会在一天中的某个时间尝试使其免受其他事物的影响，以便我可以思考一会儿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I think about there is Jeff Bezos has this approach in the morning. He just calls, he putters around. He has no meetings until I think 10:10 or something. He just wants to putter around, read the newspaper, see what's going on in email, which I'm trying to do. I really like that. That feels really good. I'm just going to putter around. I have no responsibilities in the morning.
turns.zh: 我的想法是杰夫·贝索斯早上就采用了这种方法。他只是打电话，到处闲逛。我认为直到 10 点 10 分左右他才会开会。他只是想闲逛，看看报纸，看看电子邮件里发生了什么，这也是我正在努力做的。我真的很喜欢这样。那种感觉真的很好。我只是去闲逛。早上我没有任何责任。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: I've never heard that. I'm going to adopt that language.
turns.zh: 我从来没有听说过。我将采用这种语言。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm just puttering and puttering. Elizabeth, is there anything else you wanted to touch on or leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 我只是喋喋不休。伊丽莎白，在我们进入激动人心的闪电回合之前，您还有什么想谈或留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: No, I'm ready for the exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 不，我已经准备好迎接激动人心的闪电回合了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好了，至此，我们已经进入了非常激动人心的闪电回合。第一个问题，您向其他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: It's probably a little recency bias, but I've been recommending What I Talk About When I Talk About Running by Murakami, which talks about introspection about the similarities between running and writing as sort of flow states and very meditative things. So I had read some of his fiction books and the autobiographical reflection on these types of either professions or hobbies I think is very insightful. So that's one. And then one of my longtime favorite books is A Fine Balance by Mistry. And that is just a great story of human complexity and challenge and relationships. So I'm drawn to both books and TV and film that are about humans.
turns.zh: 这可能有点新近偏见，但我一直推荐村上隆的《当我谈论跑步时我谈论什么》，其中谈到了对跑步和写作之间相似性的内省，作为一种心流状态和非常冥想的事情。所以我读过他的一些小说，以及对这些类型的职业或爱好的自传反思，我认为非常有见地。这就是其中之一。我长期以来最喜欢的书之一是 Mistry 的《A Fine Balance》。这就是一个关于人类复杂性、挑战和关系的伟大故事。所以我对有关人类的书籍、电视和电影很感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of TV and film, this is maybe a high stakes question for someone that works in Netflix, do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 说到电视和电影，这对于在 Netflix 工作的人来说可能是一个高风险的问题，您最近有最喜欢的电影或电视节目吗？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: I'm not going to name all Netflix. That feels too much like an advertisement. Film, Triangle of Sadness is phenomenal if you haven't seen it. And then I'll go Netflix for TV, Beef was I thought hysterical. I'm an Ali Wong fan, but also just a pretty unique storyline.
turns.zh: 我不会说出所有 Netflix 的名称。感觉太像广告了。如果您还没有看过电影《悲伤三角》，那它一定是非凡的。然后我会去Netflix看电视，《Beef》我觉得歇斯底里。我是黄阿丽的粉丝，但也只是一个非常独特的故事情节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think they just won a bunch of Emmys.
turns.zh: 我认为他们刚刚赢得了很多艾美奖。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: They did.
turns.zh: 他们做到了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Good picks. Next question. Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates that you are interviewing?
turns.zh: 惊人的。不错的选择。下一个问题。您有最喜欢问正在面试的候选人的面试问题吗？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: High talent density. I'm usually looking for the person who would be better in my role than I am in my role. So I often ask people what would their priorities be, what would they do differently if they had my job.
turns.zh: 人才密度高。我通常会寻找比我更适合我的角色的人。所以我经常问人们他们的优先事项是什么，如果他们有我的工作，他们会采取什么不同的做法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next question, do you have a favorite product that you recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 下一个问题，您最近发现自己真正喜欢的最喜欢的产品吗？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: So while I carry the CTO title, I live a pretty analog life. So my most recent product is a Fellow pour-over coffee maker, which is actually part of my morning ritual, which I'll now call puttering around, where I take great lengths in my coffee-making process because I find it calming. And then it's not a recent find, but I have to shout out that my Peloton is probably the favorite product I own.
turns.zh: 因此，虽然我担任首席技术官，但我的生活却相当模拟。所以我最近的产品是 Fellow 手冲咖啡机，这实际上是我早晨例行公事的一部分，我现在将其称为闲逛，我在咖啡制作过程中花费了大量时间，因为我发现它能让人平静。这并不是最近才发现的，但我必须大声说我的 Peloton 可能是我最喜欢的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The bike or the treadmill?
turns.zh: 自行车还是跑步机？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Bike. I'm a recovering outdoor cyclist, so it's also kind of questionable if I can even admit to this, but that's why I would admit to I love the Peloton despite being ideally an outdoor cyclist.
turns.zh: 自行车。我是一名正在康复中的户外自行车手，所以我是否能承认这一点也有点值得怀疑，但这就是为什么我承认我喜欢 Peloton，尽管我是一名理想的户外自行车手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have questions about your cycling, but before that question, do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to or share with friends or family that you find useful either in work or in life?
turns.zh: 我对你的骑行有疑问，但在问这个问题之前，你是否有一条最喜欢的人生格言，你经常回顾或与朋友或家人分享，你认为它在工作或生活中都很有用？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: My mom said something to me that has stuck with me. I don't know if I live it very well, but the phrase was, "Something good happens every day." And the reason she said it was because she was encouraging me to be more mindful about enjoying the small things in the day-to-day rather than letting myself get caught up in the busyness.
turns.zh: 我妈妈对我说了一些让我印象深刻的话。我不知道我是否过得很好，但那句话是“每天都会有好事发生”。她之所以这么说，是因为她鼓励我更加留意享受日常生活中的小事，而不是让自己陷入忙碌之中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful. Final question. You're a big biker and triathlete. I am curious what that sport and time has given you in your career or in life. What benefits have you found from spending so much time and energy, running, biking, being an athlete?
turns.zh: 美丽的。最后一个问题。你是一位伟大的自行车手和铁人三项运动员。我很好奇这项运动和时间给你的职业生涯或生活带来了什么。花费如此多的时间和精力跑步、骑自行车、成为一名运动员，你发现了什么好处？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Certainly by mental resilience. So while those sound like physical strength, I've found especially endurance sports are much more mental and how you go through the highs and lows and sustain and then coming back from challenge. So those sports have had their highs and lows and from the lows I've really learned how to recover and bounce back. So those feel like universally applicable skills.
turns.zh: 当然是靠心理承受能力。因此，虽然这些听起来像是身体力量，但我发现耐力运动尤其需要精神力量，以及如何经历高潮和低谷并维持，然后从挑战中恢复过来。所以这些运动都有高潮和低谷，从低谷中我真正学会了如何恢复和反弹。所以这些感觉像是普遍适用的技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have such an interesting mix of athleticism and then Netflix, what a good balance for life. This is going to give me permission to go watch Netflix recording this on Friday afternoon. Elizabeth, you're awesome. Thank you so much for being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and maybe follow up on things? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 你把运动能力和 Netflix 有趣地结合在一起，这是生活的一个很好的平衡。这将允许我在周五下午观看 Netflix 录制的视频。伊丽莎白，你太棒了。非常感谢您来到这里。最后两个问题。如果人们想要联系并跟进事情，可以在哪里找到您？听众如何对你有用？

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: You can always find me on LinkedIn, so definitely reach out or ping me if you have questions or comments. I think the way the listeners can be useful to me is being maybe curious about how they can show up even better in their lives now that we've done this reflection on Netflix culture and how we show up for other people. I would like to ask listeners to pay that forward to people that they're working with and how they show up for them.
turns.zh: 您随时可以在 LinkedIn 上找到我，因此如果您有疑问或意见，请务必联系我或联系我。我认为听众对我有用的方式可能是好奇他们如何才能在自己的生活中表现得更好，既然我们已经对 Netflix 文化以及我们如何向其他人展示自己进行了反思。我想请听众将这一点传递给与他们一起工作的人以及他们如何为他们服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I love that. If you end up doing this and you're listening, maybe leave a comment on YouTube or in Substack with something that you haven't covered about yourself. Elizabeth, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 惊人的。我喜欢那个。如果你最终这样做了并且你正在倾听，也许可以在 YouTube 或 Substack 中留下一些你没有涉及到的关于你自己的评论。伊丽莎白，非常感谢你来到这里。

turns.speaker: Elizabeth Stone
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. I hope you have a great weekend.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。我希望你周末愉快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Same. Bye everyone. (01:13:20): Thank you so much for listening. If you found this valuable, you can subscribe to the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. Also, please consider giving us a rating or leaving a review as that really helps other listeners find the podcast. You can find all past episodes or learn more about the show at lennyspodcast.com. See you in the next episode.
turns.zh: 相同的。再见大家。 (01:13:20)：非常感谢您的收听。如果您发现这很有价值，您可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify 或您最喜欢的播客应用程序上订阅该节目。另外，请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，因为这确实有助于其他听众找到播客。您可以在 lennyspodcast.com 上找到所有过去的剧集或了解有关该节目的更多信息。下一集见。
